name: NEMO deficiency (X-linked, IKBKG)
aliases: X-linked anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia with immunodeficiency

clinicalPearls: An X-linked disorder of males caused by hypomorphic mutations in IKBKG, which encodes the regulatory NEMO subunit essential for nuclear factor kappa B signalling
The classic phenotype couples anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia (sparse hair, conical or missing teeth, reduced sweating) with a broad immunodeficiency
Susceptibility spans encapsulated pyogenic bacteria, mycobacteria (including severe BCG reactions), and often opportunistic and viral pathogens, reflecting failure across multiple immune pathways
Impaired antibody responses, notably to polysaccharide antigens, are common and may be accompanied by low or dysregulated immunoglobulin levels including raised IgM in some patients
Inflammatory bowel-like colitis and other immune dysregulation can complicate the immunodeficiency
Complete loss of NEMO is lethal in males and instead causes incontinentia pigmenti in heterozygous females, so surviving affected males carry partial-function mutations
Management combines immunoglobulin replacement, antimicrobial prophylaxis, avoidance of live vaccines, and consideration of haematopoietic stem cell transplantation in severe cases
reference.pathophysiology: NEMO, the regulatory subunit of the IkappaB kinase complex encoded by IKBKG on the X chromosome, is required to activate the transcription factor nuclear factor kappa B downstream of many immune and developmental receptors, including Toll-like receptors, the interleukin-1 and tumour necrosis factor receptor families, and the ectodysplasin receptor. Because this pathway serves both immune signalling and the development of ectodermal structures, hypomorphic mutations simultaneously impair innate and adaptive immune responses and disrupt the formation of sweat glands, hair, and teeth. Weakened Toll-like receptor and cytokine signalling blunts inflammatory and antibody responses, so the host handles encapsulated bacteria, mycobacteria, and certain viruses poorly, while dysregulated signalling can also drive autoinflammation and colitis.
additionalDifferentials: Other combined immunodeficiencies with syndromic features
X-linked agammaglobulinaemia and other antibody deficiencies
Hyper-IgM syndromes (CD40 ligand and related defects)
IkappaB-alpha gain-of-function deficiency with a similar ectodermal-dysplasia-immunodeficiency picture
Autosomal recessive anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia without immunodeficiency
additionalInvestigations: Genetic sequencing of IKBKG, including assessment for common recurrent mutations and copy-number changes
Quantitative immunoglobulins with specific antibody responses to protein and polysaccharide vaccines
Functional assays of Toll-like receptor and cytokine-driven nuclear factor kappa B activation in blood cells
Lymphocyte subset and natural killer cell function analysis
Cultures and species identification for bacterial and mycobacterial infections
Clinical and dental assessment of ectodermal features and sweating
Endoscopy and histology when inflammatory colitis is suspected
redFlags: Severe or disseminated infection after BCG vaccination
Invasive infection with encapsulated bacteria in a boy with ectodermal features
Opportunistic or severe viral infection indicating broad immune failure
Chronic diarrhoea and colitis suggesting immune dysregulation
A maternal family history of male infant deaths or incontinentia pigmenti in females
reference.prognosis: Outcome varies with the specific mutation and phenotype; some patients are stabilised with immunoglobulin replacement and prophylaxis, but severe combined phenotypes carry high infective mortality, and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, while potentially curative for the immunodeficiency, is challenging and does not correct the ectodermal features.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnosis when ectodermal features are subtle or when immunodeficiency dominates the presentation
Giving live vaccines, including BCG, before the diagnosis is excluded
Interpreting a raised IgM as a simple hyper-IgM syndrome without recognising the wider signalling defect
Missing accompanying colitis or other immune dysregulation
Failing to counsel the family about X-linked inheritance and the incontinentia pigmenti link in females
references: Stiehm's Immunologic Disorders in Infants and Children
IUIS Expert Committee classification of inborn errors of immunity
management: Immunoglobulin replacement therapy to correct impaired antibody responses
Antimicrobial prophylaxis and avoidance of live vaccines, particularly BCG given the risk of severe mycobacterial reactions
Prompt aggressive treatment of infections with targeted antibacterial and antimycobacterial agents
Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation as the potentially curative option for the immunodeficiency
Management of immune dysregulation such as inflammatory colitis with immunomodulatory therapy
Supportive management of the ectodermal features, including dental care and avoidance of overheating due to reduced sweating
Coordinated care by clinical immunology and genetics, with prompt escalation for severe or opportunistic infection
Genetic counselling and family screening for the X-linked IKBKG mutation
